notes.front: What is open source software, as GitHub's docs present it?
notes.back: Software that anyone can freely use, modify and share, in modified or unmodified form.
notes.explanation: The glossary adds that the idea is often extended beyond software, to a way of collaborating in which working materials are put online for anyone to fork, modify, discuss and contribute to.
notes.example: Like a community garden: anyone may plant, weed or water, and everyone shares the harvest.
notes.evidence: Open source software is software that can be freely used, modified, and shared (in both modified and unmodified form) by anyone. Today the concept of "open source" is often extended beyond software, to represent a philosophy of collaboration in which working materials are made available online for anyone to fork, modify, discuss, and contribute to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub glossary”, “open source”

notes.front: What is the good first issue label?
notes.back: A default label that indicates a good issue for first-time contributors.
notes.explanation: It marks issues suited to people contributing for the first time.
notes.example: Like a "beginners welcome" sign on the easiest jobs in a volunteer workshop.
notes.evidence: good first issue Indicates a good issue for first-time contributors
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing labels”, “About default labels”

notes.front: What is GitHub Sponsors?
notes.back: A way for the developer community to support, with money, the people and organizations who build and maintain the open source projects they depend on.
notes.explanation: It works directly on GitHub.
notes.example: Like a tip jar for the people who keep your favourite free tools running.
notes.evidence: GitHub Sponsors allows the developer community to financially support the people and organizations who design, build, and maintain the open source projects they depend on, directly on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Sponsors”

notes.front: What does it mean to follow someone on GitHub?
notes.back: You see their public activity on your personal dashboard.
notes.explanation: If someone you follow stars a public repository, GitHub may recommend it to you; you can unfollow at any time.
notes.example: Like subscribing to a writer's newsletter to hear what they publish.
notes.evidence: When you follow people, you'll see their public activity on your personal dashboard. If someone you follow stars a public repository, GitHub may recommend the repository to you.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Following people”, “About followers”

notes.front: What is GitHub Marketplace?
notes.back: A place that connects you to developers who want to extend and improve their GitHub workflows, where free and paid tools are listed.
notes.explanation: It offers two types of tool: GitHub Actions and apps.
notes.example: Like an app store for add-ons to the way you work on GitHub.
notes.evidence: GitHub Marketplace connects you to developers who want to extend and improve their GitHub workflows. You can list free and paid tools for developers to use in GitHub Marketplace. GitHub Marketplace offers developers two types of tools: GitHub Actions and Apps
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Marketplace for apps”

notes.front: What is InnerSource?
notes.back: The application of open source practices and principles to software development within the enterprise.
notes.explanation: This is the definition given by the InnerSource Commons learning path.
notes.example: Like a company running its internal tools the way a public open source project is run, but only staff can take part.
notes.evidence: This Learning Path gives an introduction to InnerSource. InnerSource is the application of open source practices and principles to software development within the enterprise.
notes.source: InnerSource Commons, Learning Path, “Introduction”

notes.front: What is a fork on GitHub?
notes.back: A repository that starts as a copy of another repository, called the upstream repository, and stays connected to it.
notes.explanation: A fork has its own settings and permissions.
notes.example: Like photocopying a recipe book to make your own notes, while still being able to suggest changes to the original.
notes.evidence: Forks are repositories that start as copies of another repository, called the upstream repository. A fork has its own settings and permissions but stays connected to the upstream repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Forks”

notes.front: What is a topic on a GitHub repository?
notes.back: A tag added to a repository about its purpose, subject area or other qualities, to help people find and contribute to it.
notes.explanation: Topics relate to things such as a project's purpose or subject area.
notes.example: Like the subject stickers on a library book's spine.
notes.evidence: To help other people find and contribute to your project, you can add topics to your repository related to your project's intended purpose, subject area, affinity groups, or other important qualities.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Classifying your repository with topics”

notes.front: A junior developer wants to build on her technical expertise and boost her portfolio. Following GitHub's docs, what could she do?
choices: Buy a tool in GitHub Marketplace
Follow as many people as she can
notes.back: Contribute to open source projects.
notes.explanation: The docs say contributing to open source lets you build on your technical expertise and boost your portfolio.

choicesExplained.Buy a tool in GitHub Marketplace: Marketplace tools extend workflows; buying one is not contributing.
choicesExplained.Follow as many people as she can: Following shows you people's activity; it is not a contribution.
choicesExplained.Create a private repository: A private repository is only accessible to her and people she shares it with.

notes.evidence: Contributing to open source software allows you to build upon your technical expertise, boost your portfolio, help shape the future of technology, and connect with developers across the globe.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Finding ways to contribute to open source on GitHub”

notes.front: A student interested in robotics wants to find related projects and good first issues on GitHub. Which page pattern points her there?
notes.back: github.com/topics/<topic>, for example github.com/topics/robotics.
notes.explanation: The docs suggest visiting the topic page for a subject that interests you, to find relevant projects and good first issues.

choicesExplained.github.com/sponsors: That is for supporting developers with money, not finding projects by subject.
choicesExplained.github.com/marketplace: Marketplace lists actions and apps, not projects by subject.
choicesExplained.Her own repository's settings: Settings manage her own repository, not other people's projects.

notes.evidence: If there's a particular topic that interests you, visit github.com/topics/<topic> . For example, if you are interested in machine learning, you can find relevant projects and good first issues by visiting
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Finding ways to contribute to open source on GitHub”, “Using other resources to find projects to contribute to”

notes.front: Where can you find personalised recommendations of projects and good first issues, based on your past contributions and stars?
notes.back: In Explore GitHub.
notes.explanation: The recommendations are available if you have been active on GitHub.
notes.evidence: If you've been active on GitHub, you can find personalized recommendations for projects and good first issues based on your past contributions, stars, and other activities in Explore GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Finding ways to contribute to open source on GitHub”, “Using other resources to find projects to contribute to”

notes.front: Before you start contributing to an open source repository, what do the docs recommend checking?
notes.back: Whether the repository is being actively maintained.
notes.explanation: Copilot can analyse a repository and tell you about its recent activity.
notes.evidence: Before getting started contributing to an open source repository, it's recommended to check if the repository is being actively maintained. Copilot can analyze a repository and tell you about its recent activity.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Finding ways to contribute to open source on GitHub”, “Checking if the repository is actively maintained”

notes.front: Which repository page do issues labelled good first issue populate?
notes.back: The repository's contribute page.
notes.explanation: The docs point to github/docs/contribute as an example of such a page.
notes.evidence: Issues with the good first issue label are used to populate the repository's contribute page. For an example of a contribute page, see github/docs/contribute
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing labels”, “About default labels”

notes.front: A maintainer has a small, well-described typo fix she would like a newcomer to pick up as their first contribution. Which default label should she apply?
notes.back: good first issue
notes.explanation: It indicates a good issue for first-time contributors.

choicesExplained.help wanted: `help wanted` says a maintainer wants help, without marking the issue as suited to first-timers.
choicesExplained.question: `question` marks an item that needs more information.

notes.evidence: good first issue Indicates a good issue for first-time contributors help wanted Indicates that a maintainer wants help on an issue or pull request
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing labels”, “About default labels”

notes.front: When you sponsor someone through GitHub Sponsors, what kinds of payment can you choose between?
notes.back: One-time or monthly payments, in tiers set by the sponsored account.
notes.explanation: You can sponsor on behalf of your personal account or an organization.
notes.evidence: You can sponsor anyone with a sponsored developer profile or sponsored organization profile on behalf of your personal account or an organization. You can select from a range of sponsorship tiers, whether for an individual profile or multiple profiles in bulk, and choose between one-time or monthly payment amounts and benefits, all determined by the sponsored account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Sponsors”, “About GitHub Sponsors”

notes.front: GitHub Sponsors charges {{c1::no}} fees for sponsorships from personal accounts, so 100% goes to the sponsored developer or organization.
notes.back: no
notes.explanation: All of a personal-account sponsorship reaches the sponsored developer or organization.
notes.evidence: GitHub Sponsors does not charge any fees for sponsorships from personal accounts, so 100% of these sponsorships go to the sponsored developer or organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Sponsors”, “About GitHub Sponsors”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: A company sponsors an open source maintainer from its organization account, paying by credit card. What fee may GitHub Sponsors charge?
choices: Up to 6%: 3% card processing and 3% GitHub service processing
Up to 3%, for card processing only
notes.back: Up to 6%: 3% card processing and 3% GitHub service processing.
notes.explanation: Organizations can save the 3% card processing fee by switching to invoiced billing.

choicesExplained.No fee at all: No fee applies to sponsorships from personal accounts, not organization accounts.
choicesExplained.A flat 10%: The docs give a fee of up to 6%.
choicesExplained.Up to 3%, for card processing only: With card payment, the 3% GitHub service processing fee applies too.

notes.evidence: GitHub Sponsors charges a fee of up to 6% for sponsorships from organization accounts. The 6% fee is split between the following: * 3% credit card processing fee * 3% GitHub service processing fee Organizations can save the 3% credit card processing fee by switching to invoiced billing for sponsorships.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Sponsors”, “About GitHub Sponsors”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: Who is eligible to become a sponsored developer?
notes.back: Anyone who contributes to an open source project and lives in a supported region.
notes.explanation: Contributions are not limited to code: bug reports, issue triage, documentation, mentorship and design count, among others.
notes.evidence: Anyone who contributes to an open source project and lives in a supported region is eligible to become a sponsored developer. Contributions include but are not limited to bug reports, issue triage, code, documentation, leadership, business development, project management, mentorship, and design.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Sponsors”, “About GitHub Sponsors”

notes.front: A developer admires a well-known maintainer and wants to see her public activity on his own dashboard. What should he do?
notes.back: Follow her.
notes.explanation: When you follow people, you see their public activity on your personal dashboard.

choicesExplained.Star all her repositories: Starring saves repositories; it does not show her activity on his dashboard.
choicesExplained.Fork her repositories: A fork is a copy of a repository, not a feed of her activity.

notes.evidence: When you follow people, you'll see their public activity on your personal dashboard.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Following people”, “About followers”

notes.front: When you follow an organization, what are two kinds of its public activity you see on your dashboard?
notes.back: Any two of: new discussions, sponsorships, repositories.
notes.explanation: Following organizations is in public preview and subject to change.
notes.evidence: The ability to follow organizations is currently in public preview and subject to change. ## About followers When you follow organizations on GitHub, you'll see their public activity on your personal dashboard. This activity includes new discussions, sponsorships, and repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Following organizations”, “About followers”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: Who can publish an action in GitHub Marketplace?
notes.back: Anyone.
notes.explanation: GitHub verifies some partner organizations, which are shown as verified creators.
notes.evidence: Anyone can publish an action in GitHub Marketplace. GitHub verifies some partner organizations and these are shown as verified creators.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Marketplace for apps”, “GitHub Actions”

notes.front: A solo developer wants to sell a paid plan for an app she owns on her personal account through GitHub Marketplace. Can she?
choices: No: only apps owned by organizations can sell, after publisher verification
Yes, if the app is an action
No: Marketplace lists only free tools
notes.back: No: anyone can share apps for free, but only apps owned by organizations can be sold, and paid plans need publisher verification.
notes.explanation: Paid plans and a marketplace badge require the publisher verification process.

choicesExplained.Yes, once she lists it: Selling is limited to apps owned by organizations.
choicesExplained.Yes, if the app is an action: Actions and apps are different kinds of tool; the selling rule here is for apps.
choicesExplained.No: Marketplace lists only free tools: Marketplace lists free and paid tools.

notes.evidence: Anyone can share their apps with other users for free on GitHub Marketplace but only apps owned by organizations can sell their app. To publish paid plans for your app and display a marketplace badge, you must complete the publisher verification process.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Marketplace for apps”, “Apps”

notes.front: What does InnerSource encourage and reward?
notes.back: Collaboration and code reuse with anyone, whatever their position in the company's organizational structure.
notes.explanation: The InnerSource Commons learning path gives this as the problem InnerSource solves.
notes.evidence: What Problems Does InnerSource Solve? InnerSource encourages and rewards collaboration and code reuse with anyone, regardless of their position in a company’s organizational structure.
notes.source: InnerSource Commons, Learning Path, “Introduction”

notes.front: A bank's mobile team keeps waiting months for another department to add small features to a shared internal library. The bank wants teams to contribute to each other's internal code the way public projects accept contributions. What is this approach called?
notes.back: InnerSource.
notes.explanation: InnerSource Commons says it lets teams that need a feature (it calls them guest teams) get it when they need it, without taking on the long-term burden of maintaining it.

choicesExplained.Open source: Here the code stays inside the company; open source practices applied internally are InnerSource.
choicesExplained.GitHub Sponsors: GitHub Sponsors funds open source maintainers.
choicesExplained.GitHub Marketplace: GitHub Marketplace lists actions and apps.

notes.evidence: InnerSource gives a company a scalable strategy for guest teams to get feature requests when they need them without the long-term burden of maintenance.
notes.source: InnerSource Commons, Learning Path, “Introduction”

notes.front: What is the difference between a branch and a fork?
notes.back: A branch is part of one repository; a fork is a separate repository with its own settings and collaboration space.
notes.explanation: Each fork can have its own branches, issues and pull requests, labels and wikis, among other things.
notes.evidence: A branch is part of one repository. A fork is a separate repository with its own settings and collaboration space. Each fork can have its own: * Branches * Members and discussions * Issues and pull requests * Actions and projects * Tags, labels, and wikis
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Forks”, “What makes forks distinct from branches”

notes.front: Can you make a fork of a public repository private on its own?
notes.back: No: public repository forks are public, and you cannot change a fork's visibility by itself.
notes.explanation: All repositories in a repository network, the upstream and its forks, share the same visibility setting.
notes.evidence: Public repository forks are public, and private repository forks are private. You cannot change the visibility of a fork by itself. All repositories in a repository network share the same visibility setting. A repository network includes the upstream repository, its forks, and forks of those forks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Forks”, “Visibility of forks”

notes.front: Can you fork a private repository to an organization on GitHub Free?
notes.back: No; with the owner's permission you can fork it to your personal account or to a GitHub Team organization where you can create repositories.
notes.explanation: Forking a private repository also needs access to it and the owner's permission.
notes.evidence: If you have access to a private repository and the owner permits forking, you can fork the repository: * To your personal account * To an organization on GitHub Team where you have permission to create repositories You cannot fork a private repository to an organization using GitHub Free.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Forks”, “Which repositories can be forked?”

notes.front: What are the rules for creating repository topics?
notes.back: Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only; 50 characters or less; no more than 20 topics.
notes.explanation: The docs list these three rules for creating a topic.
notes.evidence: When creating a topic: * Use lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens. * Use 50 characters or less. * Add no more than 20 topics.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Classifying your repository with topics”, “About topics”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: A team adds the topic "project-nightjar" to a private repository, hoping to keep that code name secret. Is the topic name hidden?
choices: No: topic names are always public, even when created in a private repository
Yes: topics on private repositories are private
Yes, unless the repository is later made public
Only organization owners can see it
notes.back: No: topic names are always public, even when created from within a private repository.
notes.explanation: The docs give this as a note on adding topics to a repository.

choicesExplained.Yes: topics on private repositories are: The docs say topic names are always public.
choicesExplained.Yes, unless the repository is later made: The name is public from the start.
choicesExplained.Only organization owners can see it: Topic names are always public, not limited to owners.

notes.evidence: Topic names are always public, even if you create the topic from within a private repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Classifying your repository with topics”, “Adding topics to your repository”

notes.front: Which repositories does GitHub analyse to suggest topics?
notes.back: Public repositories; private repository content is not analysed and gets no topic suggestions.
notes.explanation: Repository admins can accept or reject the suggested topics.
notes.evidence: Additionally, GitHub analyzes public repository content and generates suggested topics that repository admins can accept or reject. Private repository content is not analyzed and does not receive topic suggestions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Classifying your repository with topics”, “About topics”
